Front:
Microfiltration and ultrafiltration are generally used to remove:
a. Suspended solids and microorganisms
b. Dissolved salts only
c. Only gases
d. Only color
Back: Answer: a. Suspended solids and microorganisms

Front:
MF/UF membranes are typically operated:
a. In either dead-end or cross-flow configurations
b. Only as vacuum filters
c. Only in series with sand filters
d. Without any backwash
Back: Answer: a. In either dead-end or cross-flow configurations

Front:
Transmembrane pressure (TMP) is:
permeate
a. The average pressure difference between feed/retentate and
b. The static head in the clearwell
c. The suction pressure of a pump
d. The discharge pressure of the chemical pump
Back: Answer: a. The average pressure difference between feed/retentate and

Front:
A rising TMP during MF operation usually indicates:
a. Fouling or plugging of the membrane pores
b. Loss of membrane integrity
c. Decreasing feed flow
d. Lower water temperature
Back: Answer: a. Fouling or plugging of the membrane pores

Front:
A common method to restore MF/UF performance is:
a. Backwashing and chemically enhanced backwash (CEB)
b. Increasing feed pH only
c. Adding more sand to filters
d. Reducing membrane area
Back: Answer: a. Backwashing and chemically enhanced backwash (CEB)

Front:
An integrity test for MF/UF primarily detects:
a. Fiber breaks or leaks allowing particle passage
b. TMP changes due to fouling
c. Loss of disinfectant residual
d. Changes in hardness
Back: Answer: a. Fiber breaks or leaks allowing particle passage

Front:
A pressure decay test (PDT) on MF/UF is used to:
a. Determine if air is leaking through damaged fibers
b. Measure RO recovery
c. Measure UV dose
d. Evaluate filter media depth
Back: Answer: a. Determine if air is leaking through damaged fibers

Front:
Permeate from an MF system is often used as:
a. Pretreatment feed to an RO system
b. Final product water without further treatment in all cases
c. Backwash water only
d. Sludge thickening water
Back: Answer: a. Pretreatment feed to an RO system

Front:
A low-permeate flow with normal TMP might indicate:
a. Instrument or flow meter error
b. Severe fouling
c. Fiber breaks
d. High feed turbidity
Back: Answer: a. Instrument or flow meter error

Front:
Air scour during MF backwash is primarily used to:
a. Dislodge particles from the membrane surface
b. Disinfect the membrane
c. Increase permeate recovery
d. Control pH
Back: Answer: a. Dislodge particles from the membrane surface

Front:
Chemical clean-in-place (CIP) on MF/UF membranes is performed when:
a. CEBs and backwash no longer restore TMP or flux
b. The plant shuts down daily
c. The membranes pass integrity testing
d. Turbidity is very low
Back: Answer: a. CEBs and backwash no longer restore TMP or flux

Front:
High pH cleaning solutions on MF/UF are most effective for:
a. Organic and biological fouling
b. Inorganic scaling only
c. Removing chlorine
d. Adjusting alkalinity
Back: Answer: a. Organic and biological fouling

Front:
Low pH cleaning solutions on MF/UF are most effective for:
a. Removing inorganic scales such as calcium carbonate
b. Removing biofilm only
c. Removing organics only
d. Adjusting CT
Back: Answer: a. Removing inorganic scales such as calcium carbonate

Front:
If MF filtrate turbidity suddenly increases, operators should first:
operation
a. Check integrity tests, valves, and analyzers for correct
b. Increase plant flow
c. Decrease backwash frequency
d. Turn off air scour
Back: Answer: a. Check integrity tests, valves, and analyzers for correct

Front:
Operating MF at too high a flux typically:
a. Accelerates fouling and shortens run times
b. Reduces fouling
c. Eliminates the need for backwash
d. Improves permeate quality
Back: Answer: a. Accelerates fouling and shortens run times

Front:
Recovery for an MF/UF skid is often limited by:
a. Solids loading and backwash waste requirements
b. RO feed pressure
c. UV intensity
d. Finished water pH
Back: Answer: a. Solids loading and backwash waste requirements

Front:
The primary measurement used as a pretreatment performance indicator
for RO is:
a. Silt density index (SDI) or particle index
b. Specific conductance
c. Color units
d. Alkalinity
Back: Answer: a. Silt density index (SDI) or particle index

Front:
Operating MF/UF in “submerged” mode means:
permeate side
a. Membranes are immersed in a tank and suction is applied on the
b. Membranes operate under high pressure in pressure vessels
c. Membranes are located inside the clearwell
d. Membranes are placed in the distribution system
Back: Answer: a. Membranes are immersed in a tank and suction is applied on the

Front:
A typical driving force for pressure UF is:
a. 20–60 psi (140–415 kPa)
b. 1–2 psi
c. 200–300 psi
d. Atmospheric pressure only
Back: Answer: a. 20–60 psi (140–415 kPa)

Front:
Inadequate pretreatment ahead of MF/UF may lead to:
a. Rapid fouling and shortened membrane life
b. Higher recovery
c. Lower TMP
d. Improved flux
Back: Answer: a. Rapid fouling and shortened membrane life

Front:
MF filtrate turbidity is stable, but TMP increases rapidly during
each cycle. What is the most likely cause?
a. Reversible fouling buildup between backwashes
b. Fiber break
c. Analyzer malfunction
d. Air scour failure
Back: Answer: a. Reversible fouling buildup between backwashes

Front:
MF integrity test passes, but filtrate turbidity spikes briefly
during transitions. Why?
a. Fiber failure
b. Air intrusion or bubbles reaching turbidity analyzer
c. Module breach
d. CEB under-dosing
Back: Answer: b. Air intrusion or bubbles reaching turbidity analyzer

Front:
MF backwash frequency is reduced without adjusting flux. Expected
outcome?
a. Faster TMP rise
b. Lower TMP
c. Higher filtrate turbidity
d. Lower energy use
Back: Answer: a. Faster TMP rise

Front:
MF CEB chlorine concentration is lower than target. What will
operators observe?
a. Poor chemical cleaning effectiveness
b. Higher UVT
c. Higher filtrate turbidity
d. Lower TMP
Back: Answer: a. Poor chemical cleaning effectiveness

Front:
MF TMP begins rising earlier in each filtration cycle. What is the
most likely cause?
a. Insufficient backwash frequency
b. Analyzer drift
c. Integrity failure
d. Chemical under-dosing
Back: Answer: a. Insufficient backwash frequency

Front:
MF filtrate turbidity increases slightly while TMP remains stable.
Most likely:
a. Fouling
b. Fiber break or localized leak
c. TMP probe drift
d. Low flux
Back: Answer: b. Fiber break or localized leak

Front:
MF integrity test fails with a high air decay rate. First step?
a. Verify test setup and repeat the test
b. Replace the entire rack
c. Increase flux
d. Conduct CIP
Back: Answer: a. Verify test setup and repeat the test

Front:
MF CEBs become less effective over time. Root cause?
a. High UVT
b. Chemical strength deterioration or incorrect mixing
c. Analyzer error
d. Excessive air scour
Back: Answer: b. Chemical strength deterioration or incorrect mixing

Front:
An MF train passes integrity testing, but TMP continues to rise
while filtrate turbidity remains  ≤ 0.05 NTU. What is the most
likely interpretation?
a. Gradual, reversible fouling
b. Catastrophic fiber break
c. Analyzer drift
d. Header O-ring leak
Back: Answer: a. Gradual, reversible fouling

Front:
Operators increased low-pH CEB frequency with minimal TMP
improvement. What is the best next step?
a. Switch to high-pH CEB targeting organic fouling
b. Reduce air scour
c. Reduce flux
d. Increase backwash frequency only
Back: Answer: a. Switch to high-pH CEB targeting organic fouling

Front:
For an MF system operating at constant flux, what happens when
recovery is increased?
a. Solids loading per unit membrane area increases
b. TMP decreases
c. Backwash frequency decreases
d. Integrity credit decreases
Back: Answer: a. Solids loading per unit membrane area increases

Front:
An MF integrity test shows a repeatable small leak equivalent to a
single broken fiber. If ignored, the main risk is:
a. Loss of log removal credit
b. Increased TMP
c. Shorter cycle times
d. Higher filtrate pH
Back: Answer: a. Loss of log removal credit

Front:
MF filtrate turbidity begins trending upward from 0.03 NTU to 0.07
NTU, but TMP is stable. Most likely cause?
a. Fiber break in multiple modules
b. Turbidity analyzer drift or fouling
c. Irreversible fouling
d. Backwash air scour malfunction
Back: Answer: b. Turbidity analyzer drift or fouling

Front:
MF TMP rises during the filtration cycle but resets normally after
backwash. Interpretation?
a. Reversible fouling
b. Irreversible fouling
c. Broken fibers
d. Chemical cleaning required immediately
Back: Answer: a. Reversible fouling

Front:
MF integrity test fails with a bubble point slightly below
threshold. First operator action?
a. Remove module from service
b. Repeat the integrity test
c. Perform full CEB
d. Increase flux to verify
Back: Answer: b. Repeat the integrity test

Front:
MF CEB frequency is too low. What is the likely symptom?
a. Lower TMP
b. Faster TMP rise between cycles
c. Higher filtrate turbidity
d. Improved cycle time
Back: Answer: b. Faster TMP rise between cycles

Front:
MF filtrate turbidity remains low, but TMP gradually increases from
cycle to cycle. What is the most likely cause?
a. Reversible fouling accumulating between cycles
b. Multiple fiber breaks
c. Analyzer malfunction
d. Air scour failure
Back: Answer: a. Reversible fouling accumulating between cycles

Front:
MF backwash air flow suddenly drops. Immediate likely cause?
a. Broken fibers
b. Blower or valve failure
c. High turbidity in filtrate
d. Low hypochlorite residual
Back: Answer: b. Blower or valve failure

Front:
MF integrity test passes but filtrate turbidity shows occasional
spikes. Cause?
a. Fiber break
b. Analyzer bubble interference
c. Over-fluxing
d. Permeate tank contamination
Back: Answer: b. Analyzer bubble interference

Front:
Increasing MF flux without increasing backwash frequency will most
likely lead to:
a. Lower TMP
b. Faster TMP rise
c. Higher filtrate turbidity
d. Lower energy use
Back: Answer: b. Faster TMP rise

Front:
In MF/UF systems, which operational indicator best reflects the
onset of membrane fouling?
a. A gradual increase in TMP at constant flux
b. A decrease in filtrate turbidity
c. A decrease in recovery
d. A drop in permeate conductivity
Back: Answer: a. A gradual increase in TMP at constant flux

Front:
A sudden spike in filtrate turbidity in an MF system most likely
indicates:
a. A fiber break or loss of membrane integrity
b. Low coagulant feed
c. Reduced backwash flow rate
d. Low feed alkalinity
Back: Answer: a. A fiber break or loss of membrane integrity

Front:
What is the primary purpose of a pressure decay test (PDT)?
a. To confirm membrane integrity and detect leaks or breaks
b. To adjust backwash duration
c. To optimize chemical cleaning pH
d. To measure feed SDI
Back: Answer: a. To confirm membrane integrity and detect leaks or breaks

Front:
Which condition most contributes to irreversible fouling in MF
systems?
CEB
a. Accumulation of organic matter not removed through backwash or
b. Low feed temperature
c. Elevated air scour rate
d. High flux operation only
Back: Answer: a. Accumulation of organic matter not removed through backwash or

Front:
Chemically enhanced backwash (CEB) is used primarily to:
backwash
a. Remove organic and biological foulants not removed by hydraulic
b. Restore full membrane integrity
c. Increase disinfection credit
d. Reduce permeate salinity
Back: Answer: a. Remove organic and biological foulants not removed by hydraulic

Front:
Which parameter is most important to control to reduce particulate
fouling in MF systems?
a. Silt density index (SDI) of the influent
b. Alkalinity
c. pH
d. Turbidity only
Back: Answer: a. Silt density index (SDI) of the influent

Front:
Which MF cleaning strategy is used to remove inorganic scale?
a. Acid-based chemical cleaning
b. High-pH cleaning
c. Chlorination
d. Air scouring only
Back: Answer: a. Acid-based chemical cleaning

Front:
The primary purpose of air scour during MF backwashing is to:
a. Dislodge accumulated solids on the membrane surface
b. Remove dissolved organics
c. Reduce pH
d. Increase flux beyond design limits
Back: Answer: a. Dislodge accumulated solids on the membrane surface

Front:
What is the most likely cause of a rapid TMP increase during a
single filtration cycle? *a. A sudden increase in feed solids
loading
b. Low permeability of aged membranes
c. Elevated pH
d. A failed CEB pump
Back: Answer: (not marked)

Front:
A fiber break in MF/UF is typically confirmed by:
integrity test
a. Elevated filtrate particle counts or turbidity during an
b. High permeate TDS
c. Reduced feed pressure
d. Increased backwash frequency
Back: Answer: a. Elevated filtrate particle counts or turbidity during an

Front:
Which factor most improves MF/UF membrane life expectancy? *a.
Operating within the recommended flux and TMP limits
b. Using only water for backwashing
c. Increasing recovery above design
d. Operating at maximum pressure
Back: Answer: (not marked)

Front:
Which condition most increases the frequency of CEBs?
a. High organic loading in the feedwater
b. Low temperature
c. High pH
d. Low air scour flow
Back: Answer: a. High organic loading in the feedwater

Front:
The purpose of a CIP (Clean-in-Place) in MF systems is to:
hydraulic cleaning
a. Restore permeability by removing foulants not removed by CEB or
b. Reduce TMP permanently to zero
c. Change membrane pore size
d. Remove silica only
Back: Answer: a. Restore permeability by removing foulants not removed by CEB or

Front:
During backwash, what does an increase in required backwash pressure
indicate?
a. Fouling or clogging of membrane pores
b. Reduced feed TDS
c. Lower pH
d. Air in permeate headers
Back: Answer: a. Fouling or clogging of membrane pores

Front:
Which variable most strongly influences MF membrane flux?
a. Water temperature
b. Permeate pH
c. Chlorine concentration
d. Turbidity alone
Back: Answer: a. Water temperature

Front:
A low air scour rate during backwash has what effect?
a. Reduced removal of accumulated solids
b. Increased permeate salinity
c. Higher recovery
d. Reduced TMP
Back: Answer: a. Reduced removal of accumulated solids

Front:
What is a typical design purpose of equalization upstream of MF?
a. To provide stable feed quality and minimize fouling events
b. To chlorinate the water thoroughly
c. To reduce TDS prior to RO
d. To maximize silica solubility
Back: Answer: a. To provide stable feed quality and minimize fouling events

Front:
MF filtrate quality is primarily measured using:
a. Turbidity or particle counts
b. pH
c. Chlorine dose
d. TDS
Back: Answer: a. Turbidity or particle counts

Front:
Which MF operational condition most directly increases fouling rate?
a. Operating above design flux
b. High permeate temperature
c. Low recovery
d. High air scour rate
Back: Answer: a. Operating above design flux

Front:
Which scenario most likely requires immediate removal of an MF unit
from service?
integrity
a. Failure of pressure decay testing indicating compromised
b. TMP rising 0.1 psi above baseline
c. Slight increase in filtrate turbidity under 0.05 NTU
d. Backwash pump operating at reduced efficiency
Back: Answer: a. Failure of pressure decay testing indicating compromised

Front:
In a microfiltration (MF) system used upstream of RO, which
operational indicator best reflects the onset of membrane fouling?
flux.
a. Permeate conductivity decreases.
b. Transmembrane pressure (TMP) gradually increases at constant
c. Recovery increases above the design limit.
d. Feed pH decreases below the target value.
Back: Answer: b. Transmembrane pressure (TMP) gradually increases at constant

Front:
What is the primary purpose of conducting a membrane integrity test
(MIT) on MF or UF membranes used in potable reuse?
passage.
a. To determine whether the membranes require chemical cleaning.
b. To measure the salt rejection performance under variable flows.
c. To verify that no breaches exist that would allow pathogen
d. To evaluate long-term scaling tendencies in the RO system.
Back: Answer: c. To verify that no breaches exist that would allow pathogen

Front:
A plant monitoring its MF system observes a rapid increase in TMP
during a single filtration cycle. Which operational issue does this
most likely indicate?
a. Gradual fouling over several days.
b. Loss of membrane structural integrity.
c. Sudden particulate breakthrough or excessive solids loading.
d. Underfeeding of coagulant upstream.
Back: Answer: c. Sudden particulate breakthrough or excessive solids loading.

Front:
A sudden increase in MF filtrate turbidity indicates:
a. Scaling inside the permeate piping.
b. Potential membrane integrity failure or fiber break.
c. Decreased feed temperature.
d. Excessive peroxide residual from upstream AOP.
Back: Answer: b. Potential membrane integrity failure or fiber break.

Front:
In MF operations, backwashing is primarily performed to:
flux.
a. Reduce permeate salinity.
b. Remove accumulated solids from membrane surfaces to restore
c. Increase recovery above design limits.
d. Improve final disinfection effectiveness.
Back: Answer: b. Remove accumulated solids from membrane surfaces to restore

Front:
A MF system displays stable TMP but a significant decrease in
filtrate flow. What operational issue is most likely?
a. Membrane fouling.
b. Irreversible clogging of feed channels.
c. Flow meter calibration error or valve restriction downstream.
d. Loss of membrane integrity.
Back: Answer: c. Flow meter calibration error or valve restriction downstream.

Front:
In MF systems, fiber breaks are typically detected by:
a. A decrease in TMP.
b. A sudden increase in filtrate turbidity or particle counts.
c. A gradual increase in flux.
d. Reduced backwash frequency.
Back: Answer: b. A sudden increase in filtrate turbidity or particle counts.

Front:
In MF/UF systems, the clean-in-place (CIP) procedure is initiated
when:
a. TMP decreases below the baseline.
b. Permeate turbidity decreases.
c. TMP rises to a predetermined threshold above baseline.
d. Recovery exceeds design value.
Back: Answer: c. TMP rises to a predetermined threshold above baseline.

Front:
In MF operations, what is the impact of excessively long filtration
cycles?
a. Reduced need for chemical cleaning.
b. Decrease in membrane permeability.
c. Increased solids loading leading to higher TMP rise.
d. Improved filtrate quality.
Back: Answer: c. Increased solids loading leading to higher TMP rise.

Front:
In MF/UF systems, air scouring during backwash is primarily used to:
a. Reduce pH in the membrane tank.
b. Remove dissolved solids.
c. Dislodge accumulated particles from the membrane surface.
d. Restore membrane integrity.
Back: Answer: c. Dislodge accumulated particles from the membrane surface.

Front:
The “headloss” across a membrane system primarily depends on:
a. Flow rate, viscosity, and fouling
b. Total hardness only
c. Chlorine residual
d. Color of the water
Back: Answer: a. Flow rate, viscosity, and fouling
